plain: The real amounts you earned and spent, as opposed to what you planned.
example: For example, we compare actuals to our budget each month to see if we are overspending on travel.

plain: The legal paper filed with the state that creates your nonprofit.
example: For example, we filed our articles of incorporation before we applied for our first grant.

plain: A review of your finances by an outside accountant to check that they are accurate.
example: For example, our audit found that our records were sound and gave us tips to track grants better.

plain: A report showing what your group owns and what it owes on a certain day.
example: For example, our balance sheet shows our cash in the bank and a bill we still need to pay.

plain: The written rules for how your organization and its board run.
example: For example, our bylaws say how many board members we need and how they are chosen.

plain: Steps that make your group stronger, like training, better systems, or more staff.
example: For example, our capacity building this year includes training for our team on writing grant reports.

plain: Working one on one with a person to set goals and connect them to services.
example: For example, our case management helps a participant find a job, housing, and counseling.

plain: A group or person who brings others together to work on a shared goal.
example: For example, as a convener, we host a monthly meeting where partners plan how to respond to shootings together.

plain: People with life experience like your participants, who earn trust and can guide them away from violence.
example: For example, our credible messengers once lived through street conflict and now mentor young people at risk.

plain: How accurate, complete, and consistent your information is.
example: For example, we improved data quality by using one form so every worker records contacts the same way.

plain: All the groups and agencies in your area that work on the same issue.
example: For example, our local ecosystem includes hospitals, schools, police, and other violence intervention groups.

plain: Outside experts who study how well your program works.
example: For example, we hired external evaluators from a local university to study our mentoring program.

plain: Rules that protect your money, like needing two people to approve a payment.
example: For example, our financial controls require two signatures on any check over $500.

plain: Your best guesses about future income and spending.
example: For example, our financial projections show we may run short of cash next spring if a grant is late.

plain: The 12-month period your organization uses for its budget and financial reports.
example: For example, our fiscal year runs from July 1 to June 30, so our audit begins in the summer.

plain: The different sources your money comes from.
example: For example, our funding streams include a city contract, two foundations, and local donors.

plain: The group of people, like a board, who guide and oversee your organization.
example: For example, our governing body meets monthly to review the budget and support our director.

plain: Help given as goods, time, or space instead of cash.
example: For example, a church gives us in-kind support by letting us use its hall for community healing circles.

plain: A report showing how much money came in and went out over a period of time.
example: For example, our income statement shows we spent more on salaries this quarter than we planned.

plain: A plan for who will lead if your top leader leaves or steps down.
example: For example, our leadership succession plan names who steps in if our director is out for a long time.

plain: A short list of questions you want to answer to get better at your work.
example: For example, our learning agenda asks which outreach hours help us reach the most high-risk young people.

plain: Knowledge gained from going through something yourself.
example: For example, staff with lived experience of incarceration help young people see a different path.

plain: A simple chart that shows how your activities lead to the changes you want to see.
example: For example, our logic model shows how street outreach leads to fewer retaliation shootings.

plain: A budget that looks ahead more than one year.
example: For example, our multi-year budget shows we will need to hire a case manager in year two.

plain: The process of welcoming and training a new staff member.
example: For example, our onboarding includes a first-week plan and a buddy who shadows the new outreach worker.

plain: The changes that result from your work.
example: For example, one outcome we track is whether participants stay out of violent conflicts for six months.

plain: The things you do and count, like events held or people served.
example: For example, our outputs this month were 40 home visits and 12 mediations.

plain: Check-ins where a supervisor talks with staff about how their work is going.
example: For example, we hold performance evaluations twice a year to share praise and set goals.

plain: Money set aside for emergencies or slow times.
example: For example, our reserves helped us make payroll when a city payment came two months late.

plain: A written plan for how you will raise the money and other support you need.
example: For example, our resource development plan lists the funders we will ask and when.

plain: Money that a funder says must be spent only on certain things.
example: For example, a restricted grant can pay for hospital-based violence intervention but not for rent.

plain: People or groups who care about or are affected by your work.
example: For example, our stakeholders include residents, funders, school staff, and the families we serve.

plain: Small set payments for time or work that are not regular wages.
example: For example, we paid stipends to young people who helped plan the summer peace event.

plain: A written plan for where your group wants to be in a few years and how it will get there.
example: For example, our strategic plan sets goals for growing from two outreach workers to six over three years.

plain: Plans to keep your work going over the long run.
example: For example, our sustainability strategies include building a savings fund and finding funders who commit for three years.

plain: Money you can spend on whatever your group needs most.
example: For example, unrestricted gifts let us pay for a van repair when a program grant cannot.

plain: Step-by-step lists of who will do what and by when.
example: For example, our work plans list who runs the youth mentoring group each week and when we review it.
